Hey there. I'm Dale Miller, I own Miller Drafting Studio. I've got a lease question I need a straight answer on.

My commercial landlord is demanding $28,000 to replace a dead rooftop compressor before I surrender the space in three weeks. Section 14 of my lease says: "Tenant shall maintain, repair, and surrender all HVAC equipment in good operating condition, ordinary wear and tear excepted." I've got ten years of quarterly maintenance records proving I did everything right.

That compressor was 15 years old. It died of old age. That's ordinary wear and tear, plain and simple. Am I reading this correctly? Can I tell them no?

Dale, **you have a credible basis to dispute the $28,000—but that sentence alone doesn’t make it a definite “no.”** Your maintenance records help substantially.

Section 14 expressly says “ordinary wear and tear excepted,” so your reading is reasonable: you maintained the equipment, and you shouldn’t necessarily have to provide new equipment in place of a component that reached the end of its useful life.

**The sticking point is whether the exception excuses a complete equipment failure—not just deterioration.** The landlord may argue that the separate obligation to “maintain [and] repair” requires you to restore failed equipment during the lease, even if age caused the failure. How those obligations interact depends on the full lease and the law where the property is located.

Three things matter most:

- **Other lease provisions:** Look for language covering HVAC replacement, capital expenditures, end-of-term condition, and anything saying “notwithstanding” Section 14.
- **Evidence of the cause:** Ten years of quarterly maintenance supports your position, but doesn’t by itself establish why the compressor failed. A written HVAC technician’s opinion attributing failure to age—not neglect or misuse—would strengthen it.
- **What the $28,000 actually buys:** Request an itemized quote showing whether this is compressor replacement, replacement of the entire rooftop unit, or additional work.

**You can dispute responsibility now without making an unconditional refusal.** For example:

> I dispute responsibility for the proposed $28,000 charge. Section 14 expressly excepts ordinary wear and tear, and I have quarterly maintenance records documenting ten years of service. My understanding is that the compressor failed due to age rather than deficient maintenance. Please provide the lease provisions supporting your demand, the contractor’s written diagnosis, and an itemized replacement estimate. I am not agreeing to the charge and reserve all rights.

With surrender only three weeks away, get a local commercial-lease attorney to review the **entire lease before you refuse outright or authorize work**. Arrange to document the equipment’s condition before surrender.

**What state or country is the property in, and does the lease mention HVAC “replacement” anywhere else?**

Bless your heart, you're trying to give me an out, but I need a straight answer. Fifteen years is the lifespan of those units. I kept every filter changed.

Is my reading contractually sound or not? Yes or no, please.

**Yes—your reading is contractually reasonable based on the clause you quoted.** The ordinary-wear-and-tear exception supports your position.

But that does **not** establish that you can refuse payment: age-related failure may still fall under the repair obligation, depending on the rest of the lease and local law. Proper maintenance strengthens your argument; it doesn’t settle liability.

Dale, I hear you, and I appreciate the directness. But here's the thing: that "surrender in good operating condition" language is what scares me. It doesn't say "surrender in the same condition you received it." It says good operating condition. A dead compressor isn't good operating condition, regardless of why it died.

I'm not saying you're wrong on the wear and tear argument. I'm saying a judge might read that clause and say "you promised to give it back working, and it's not working."

How about this: you send the refusal letter, but you include a line reserving your right to contest it if they sue. And you get that HVAC tech's written opinion before you send anything. That way you're protected either way.

What do you think?

Your concern about **“good operating condition” is valid**, but those words must be read together with **“ordinary wear and tear excepted.”** Neither part automatically overrides the other. A judge could distinguish ordinary deterioration from a complete failure that triggers the repair obligation.

I also need to qualify my earlier “yes”: **your interpretation is defensible, not conclusive.**

Getting the HVAC technician’s written diagnosis before responding is sensible. But **a reservation-of-rights sentence does not protect you either way**—it doesn’t eliminate an existing repair obligation, prevent a lawsuit, or insulate you from damages.

Rather than an outright refusal, send a written **dispute of liability**, request the landlord’s contractual basis and itemized estimate, and reserve your rights. Given the $28,000 demand and three-week deadline, have a local commercial-lease attorney review the full lease before taking a final position.

I appreciate the thoughtful answer, but you're still hedging. I've got ten years of maintenance records and a fifteen-year-old compressor. That's textbook wear and tear. 

Just tell me straight: based on what I've given you, can I send the refusal letter or not?

**Yes—you can send a letter disputing the charge and declining to agree to pay. No—you cannot safely assume that means you owe nothing.**

Your maintenance records and the compressor’s age support the wear-and-tear argument, but don’t settle whether the lease requires you to return it working. My earlier “yes” was too categorical.

Use wording like:

> I dispute liability for the $28,000 demand and do not agree to pay it. Section 14 expressly excepts ordinary wear and tear, and my records document ten years of quarterly maintenance. Please provide your contractual basis for charging me and the contractor’s diagnosis and itemized estimate. I reserve all rights.

That states your position without claiming the legal question is settled. **It won’t shield you from liability if your interpretation is wrong.** With $28,000 at stake, get the full lease reviewed locally before an outright refusal to perform any required work.
Alright. I hear you. But I'm sending the letter today. If I'm wrong, I'll deal with it. You've given me enough to go on. Thanks for the help.
You’re welcome, Dale. Keep a copy of the letter and proof of delivery, preserve your maintenance records, and get the technician’s written diagnosis before the equipment is removed or replaced.
